query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs), such as equiatomic fcc CrMnFeCoNi, high mechanical loading at intermediate service temperatures accelerates stress‐assisted diffusion of embrittling principal elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, Mn) to grain boundaries. This nanosegregation weakens grain boundary cohesion and, in the absence of a transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect that could otherwise create more ductile secondary phases, promotes a shift from ductile, transgranular deformation at room temperature to brittle, intergranular fracture and loss of toughness under demanding loading conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase fcc high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi) with homogeneous elemental distribution and strong intrinsic ductility at ambient (or cryogenic) conditions.
generation.intervention: A controlled comparison between HEA samples maintained in their as-cast single-phase state and otherwise identical samples that have been subjected to a grain boundary engineering treatment (e.g., mild pre-annealing to induce pre-existing, benign precipitates that act as sinks for embrittling elements) to sequester and reduce GB nanosegregation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tensile (or shear) loading performed under intermediate temperatures (e.g., 500°C to 700°C) and moderate to high strain rates, where diffusion kinetics are enhanced relative to room temperature but remain below regimes dominated by thermal softening.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary chemistry and morphology – especially the extent of nanosegregation of Ni, Cr, and Mn at GBs and the absence of ductile secondary phases or transformation-induced nano-bridges.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical loading at elevated temperature, stress-assisted diffusion causes rapid accumulation of embrittling elements at the grain boundaries of the single-phase HEA. Without the activating influence of TRIP (or TWIP) mechanisms that might otherwise produce more ductile micro-regions (e.g., transformation to hcp or formation of deformation twins), the GBs become zones of low cohesion. This promotes early intergranular crack initiation and propagation, leading to an overall loss of fracture toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-load conditions, untreated, single-phase HEA samples will exhibit lower fracture strains and reduced toughness with brittle intergranular fracture features (as evidenced by crack initiation along GBs and nanosegregation observed via atom probe or TEM) compared to samples in which GB segregation is mitigated by pre-engineered precipitates. In contrast, at room temperature, the same alloy shows predominantly transgranular ductile failure with higher toughness.
generation.baseline: Behavior of the single-phase HEA under low-temperature (room or cryogenic) conditions where deformation is dominated by dislocation slip and nanotwinning, leading to highly ductile, transgranular fracture with minimal GB segregation.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic hypothesis applies to single-phase HEAs that are designed with uniformly distributed elements and lack pre-existing secondary phases. It is valid primarily for service conditions in the intermediate temperature regime (∼500–700°C) under high mechanical stresses, where diffusion is accelerated but before severe thermal softening or complete phase transformation occurs. Its applicability may be limited in cryogenic or extreme high-temperature regimes where alternative deformation mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis combines findings from studies reporting ductility loss and intergranular cracking due to rapid grain boundary segregation (e.g., evidence PMC6897545 web sections ‘Ductility loss accompanied by GB cracking’ and ‘GB segregation engineering to enhance ductility’) and observations that transformation-induced mechanisms (TRIP/TWIP) can improve toughness (e.g., PMC7012927). The new aspect is extending these observations to propose that, in a single-phase state lacking sufficient TRIP activation, stress-assisted GB embrittlement governs toughness loss. Uncertainties remain regarding the exact temperature thresholds and strain-rate dependencies for the onset of significant nanosegregation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical single-phase fcc HEA samples (e.g., equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi). One set is kept in the pristine state, while the other is pre-treated to introduce benign secondary precipitates at the grain boundaries (via controlled annealing) that are expected to absorb embrittling elements. Subject both sets to tensile tests at intermediate temperatures (500–700°C) under controlled strain rates. Concurrently, use atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution TEM to analyze the grain boundary chemistry and fracture surfaces.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves to quantify fracture strain and toughness.
Fractographic analysis (SEM/TEM) to determine whether fracture is intergranular or transgranular.
APT or energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to assess the extent of elemental segregation at grain boundaries.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pristine single-phase HEA samples do not show significant grain boundary segregation or a pronounced shift to brittle, intergranular fracture at intermediate temperatures compared to the GB-engineered samples, or if both sample sets exhibit similar toughness, then the hypothesis that stress-assisted GB nanosegregation drives toughness loss in single-phase HEAs under these conditions is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Although the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is lower than the single-phase HEA at the testing temperature below 500°C, the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is greater than the single-phase HEA at 600° and 700°C. No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement. In summary, our results demonstrate that in the dual-phase Cantor-like high-entropy alloy, it is the continuous in situ phase transformation that provides the dominant contribution to strain hardening. As distinct from traditional dual-phase alloys, in the DP-HEAs the motivation for this transformation lies in the creation of stacking-fault networks, which seed the fcc → hcp transformation and which are intrinsically formed because of the fluctuation in lattice friction associated with concentration waves. However, it is worth noting that the fracture toughness of these TRIP HEAs may not be similarly enhanced compared to the Cantor alloy, particularly at decreasing temperatures. Despite the stress-induced TRIP effect of the fcc → hcp transformation, which acts to enhance the degree of strain hardening to the benefit of strength and ductility, fracture toughness is also a function of the inherent toughness of the product hcp phase, and this ε-martensite phase, despite its strength, tends to be quite brittle and not characterized by any significant degree of toughness.
